course_title: Developing Mobile Apps with Flutter Specialization

screens.title: Structured Local Data with SQLite (sqflite)
screens.subtitle: When to choose a local relational database and how to use sqflite in Flutter

narration.text: In this chapter you'll learn why a lightweight relational database like SQLite matters for mobile apps, and how the sqflite plugin lets Flutter apps read and write structured data on the device. We'll build mental models that show when shared preferences are no longer enough, and then walk through a practical Todo example: a Dart model class, a small DatabaseHelper that opens and initializes a file-based database, and the core CRUD operations you need to persist objects. Along the way you'll see how booleans map to integers in SQLite, why a primary key matters, and where to add migration logic when your schema evolves. These skills matter because many apps — note-taking, contact managers, expense trackers — store lists of structured objects and need queries, sorting, and stable identifiers. By the end of this lesson you'll understand the basic lifecycle of using sqflite: open the database, create tables, perform inserts, queries, updates and deletes, and close or upgrade the database safely. Keep an eye out for common mistakes like forgetting to await Futures or storing booleans without conversion. Ready to explore the code and try a hands-on refactor?

keyIdea.title: Why use sqflite?
keyIdea.text: Use sqflite when your app needs structured, queryable records that key-value storage cannot manage reliably.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will identify when shared preferences are insufficient and confidently integrate sqflite into a Flutter project. You will design a simple database schema, implement a Dart model with toMap and fromMap methods, and write a DatabaseHelper that opens a file-based SQLite database and creates tables. You'll perform the fundamental CRUD operations: create new records, read and map results back into model objects, update existing rows using where clauses, and delete rows safely. Finally, you will understand the basics of database migration so you can evolve the schema without losing user data. These skills matter because many mobile apps manage lists of structured data where queries, stable IDs, and schema evolution are essential. A concrete example you will practice is refactoring a To-Do app to use a Todo model stored in a todos table with an integer primary key and an integer-backed boolean column. We'll also check common pitfalls, such as not awaiting Futures or storing booleans directly instead of converting them. These objectives prepare you to persist structured local data reliably and to add migrations when your app grows.

screens.title: When to use SQLite instead of shared_preferences
screens.subtitle: Understanding the limits of key-value storage and the benefits of a relational file-based database

narration.text: Shared preferences is a lightweight key-value store intended for small pieces of app configuration: theme choice, onboarding flags, or small tokens. It stores primitive values keyed by strings and is fast and simple. However, when your app needs to manage lists of structured objects — for example, a note with a title, body, timestamp and tags, or an expense record with amount, category, and receipt references — key-value storage becomes awkward and brittle. You end up serializing lists into a single JSON string, which complicates queries, sorting, and incremental updates. SQLite is a lightweight, file-based relational database that stores rows and columns in tables. It supports S Q L queries, efficient filtering, and stable primary keys. Because the database lives in a file on the device, it requires no separate server process, yet it supports S Q L semantics like WHERE clauses and indexed lookups. Use SQLite when you need efficient queries, to persist many structured records, or when records must be individually updated or deleted. A common misconception is that SQLite is heavy for mobile; in reality, SQLite is intentionally lightweight and ideal for embedded use. The key takeaway: choose shared_preferences for small key-value settings; choose sqflite-backed SQLite when you need structured, queryable, and stable records.

keyIdea.title: Decision rule
keyIdea.text: If you manage lists of structured objects requiring queries, use a relational database; reserve shared_preferences for small config flags.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › When to use SQLite
Definition and contrast
Why a relational database solves problems that key-value cannot.
  • Shared preferences stores primitives by key; it's great for single settings and small state.
  • SQLite stores rows in tables, enabling queries, filters, and individual row updates.
  • Typical use cases for SQLite: note apps, contact managers, expense trackers — any app with many objects and fields.
  • SQLite is file-based and requires no separate server daemon, making it ideal for mobile devices.
Example
A Todo list with title, description, isCompleted and stable id needs SQLite to support queries and individual updates.
Misconception
SQLite is heavy. In fact, it is optimized for embedded use and is the correct choice for structured local data.
Quick decision checklist
  1. Do you store lists of objects with multiple fields? Use SQLite.
  2. Do you need to query, sort, or filter locally? Use SQLite.
  3. Is it just a single setting or flag? shared_preferences is fine.
Key Takeaway

Choose the tool that matches your data complexity. SQLite via sqflite gives structure, queries, and reliable IDs for local app data.

screens.title: Add sqflite and prepare the database file
screens.subtitle: Dependencies, obtaining a path, and opening a database connection

narration.text: Before you can use SQLite in Flutter you add two packages: sqflite for database APIs and path_provider to discover a safe directory for the database file. Update your pubspec. yaml and run flutter pub get; this installs the plugins your Dart code will import. The lifecycle of working with sqflite begins with locating a database path and calling openDatabase. The typical pattern is to use getDatabasesPath from sqflite or path_provider to compute a reliable location and then join that path with a filename such as todo_app. db. When opening the database you pass a version and onCreate callback. onCreate runs once when the file is first created and is where you execute CREATE TABLE statements to define the schema. You can also provide onUpgrade to handle migrations later. Always treat the database open call as asynchronous and await the returned Database object. A common mistake is not awaiting the open call or performing database operations before the database is ready; this leads to runtime errors. In short: add dependencies, compute a path, await openDatabase with onCreate, then use the returned Database to execute S Q L or use helper methods to run queries.

keyIdea.title: Open sequence
keyIdea.text: Install sqflite and path_provider, compute a file path, and await openDatabase with onCreate to initialize your tables.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Setup & Open
Dependency & path
Add these entries to pubspec.yaml and run flutter pub get to install the packages.
dependencies:
  flutter:
    sdk: flutter
  sqflite: ^2.3.0
  path_provider: ^2.1.1
Then in code, compute the path and open the database. Always await the returned Database instance before using it.
Open and initialize
Example pattern for opening a file database and creating tables.
// inside a helper
String documentsDirectory = await getDatabasesPath();
String path = join(documentsDirectory, 'todo_app.db');

return await openDatabase(
  path,
  version: 1,
  onCreate: (db, version) async {
    await db.execute(
      '''
      CREATE TABLE todos(
        id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
        title TEXT NOT NULL,
        description TEXT NOT NULL,
        isCompleted INTEGER NOT NULL
      )
      '''
    );
  },
);
Note the onCreate callback defines your initial schema. Treat this as the canonical place to run CREATE TABLE statements for a fresh database file.

screens.title: Designing the Todo model
screens.subtitle: A Dart model class with toMap and fromMap for serialization

narration.text: A model class represents the structure of the data you persist. For our Todo example the model includes id, title, description, and isCompleted. The id is nullable when constructing new todos because the database will assign an autoincrement value on insert. toMap converts a Todo to a Map where keys match your database column names; fromMap reconstructs a Todo from a query result Map. A key detail for SQLite is booleans: SQLite commonly stores booleans as integers, so your toMap should convert true to 1 and false to 0, and fromMap should convert the integer back to a boolean. Implementing toString is optional but helpful for debugging during development. Keep the model focused: it should know only how to serialize and deserialize itself, not perform database logic. This separation makes testing easier and keeps DatabaseHelper responsibilities clear. A common misconception is to put S Q L logic inside the model; instead, limit the model to data shape and conversion helpers. The model below is the exact structure you will use when implementing DatabaseHelper CRUD methods so that insert returns an id and queries return fully-formed Todo objects.

keyIdea.title: Model responsibility
keyIdea.text: A model class converts between Dart objects and Maps that match your database columns; convert booleans to integers for storage.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Todo Model
Todo model code
This class maps directly to the todos table and handles boolean conversion.
// models/todo.dart
class Todo {
  final int? id; // Nullable for new todos before insertion
  final String title;
  final String description;
  final bool isCompleted;

  Todo({
    this.id,
    required this.title,
    required this.description,
    this.isCompleted = false,
  });

  Map<String, dynamic> toMap() {
    return {
      'id': id,
      'title': title,
      'description': description,
      'isCompleted': isCompleted ? 1 : 0,
    };
  }

  @override
  String toString() {
    return 'Todo{id: $id, title: $title, description: $description, isCompleted: $isCompleted}';
  }

  factory Todo.fromMap(Map<String, dynamic> map) {
    return Todo(
      id: map['id'],
      title: map['title'],
      description: map['description'],
      isCompleted: map['isCompleted'] == 1,
    );
  }
}

screens.title: DatabaseHelper: singleton and open logic
screens.subtitle: A centralized class that manages the Database instance and lifecycle

narration.text: DatabaseHelper centralizes database access so the rest of your app calls the same instance. The common pattern is a private constructor with a single static instance and a nullable Database field that is initialized on demand. The getter for database returns the existing Database if available or calls an _initDatabase method to open and create the file. This avoids opening multiple connections and makes it easy to mock or extend later. In _initDatabase you compute the database path, call openDatabase with version, onCreate, and optionally onUpgrade. onCreate executes CREATE TABLE S Q L that matches your model's columns. Because openDatabase is asynchronous, all public methods in DatabaseHelper return Futures; callers must await them to avoid race conditions. Keep DatabaseHelper focused on S Q L and CRUD; do not mix UI code here. Also remember to choose an appropriate conflictAlgorithm for inserts; ConflictAlgorithm. replace can simplify cases where you re-insert items with existing ids. A misconception is to create database connections inside widgets: instead, use a helper so widgets only call methods like insertTodo and getTodos. This simple architecture improves testability and reduces concurrency bugs.

keyIdea.title: Single source of truth
keyIdea.text: Use a singleton DatabaseHelper to open the file-based database once and expose asynchronous CRUD methods.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › DatabaseHelper
Singleton pattern
A shared instance prevents multiple open connections and centralizes schema management.
class DatabaseHelper {
  static final DatabaseHelper _instance = DatabaseHelper._internal();
  static Database? _database;

  factory DatabaseHelper() => _instance;
  DatabaseHelper._internal();

  Future<Database> get database async {
    if (_database != null) return _database!;
    _database = await _initDatabase();
    return _database!;
  }
}
_initDatabase responsibilities
Compute path, call openDatabase, handle onCreate and onUpgrade for migrations.
  • Use getDatabasesPath and join to build the file location.
  • Pass a version number and implement onCreate to execute CREATE TABLE statements.
  • Implement onUpgrade to alter schemas when releasing new app versions.

screens.title: CRUD operations: insert, query, update, delete
screens.subtitle: Concrete DatabaseHelper methods that map to the Todo model

narration.text: CRUD is an acronym for Create, Read, Update, and Delete — the fundamental operations you perform on persisted records. In sqflite you implement these using insert, query, update, and delete calls on a Database instance. For Create, use db. insert with a table name and a map derived from your model's toMap method; using ConflictAlgorithm. replace is safe when you want new data to overwrite an existing row with the same primary key. For Read, db. query returns a List >; map those results to your model with Todo. fromMap. For Update, use db. update with a where clause 'id =?' and a matching whereArgs list; this targets a single row by primary key. For Delete, call db. delete with the same where clause. Importantly, all these operations are asynchronous: await them and update UI state only after the Future completes. A common mistake is to mutate UI state before awaiting the database call, which can cause inconsistency when an operation fails. After each write operation, reload the data or update the in-memory list with the returned values to keep the UI consistent. The code example demonstrates each method you will call from your UI layer.

keyIdea.title: CRUD pattern
keyIdea.text: Use db.insert, db.query, db.update, and db.delete with model mapping to persist and retrieve Todo objects.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › CRUD Operations
Create & Read
Insert a Todo and read all Todos from the table.
Future<int> insertTodo(Todo todo) async {
  final db = await database;
  return await db.insert(
    'todos',
    todo.toMap(),
    conflictAlgorithm: ConflictAlgorithm.replace,
  );
}

Future<List<Todo>> getTodos() async {
  final db = await database;
  final List<Map<String, dynamic>> maps = await db.query('todos');
  return List.generate(maps.length, (i) => Todo.fromMap(maps[i]));
}
Update & Delete
Target rows using where and whereArgs based on the primary key.
Future<int> updateTodo(Todo todo) async {
  final db = await database;
  return await db.update(
    'todos',
    todo.toMap(),
    where: 'id = ?',
    whereArgs: [todo.id],
  );
}

Future<int> deleteTodo(int id) async {
  final db = await database;
  return await db.delete(
    'todos',
    where: 'id = ?',
    whereArgs: [id],
  );
}
Key Takeaway

Always await database operations, map rows to model objects, and reload or update UI state after each write to keep the app consistent.

screens.title: Handling booleans and common mistakes
screens.subtitle: Why booleans need conversion and other frequent pitfalls

narration.text: A very common source of bugs is assuming SQLite supports a native boolean type. SQLite represents values with a small set of storage classes and commonly stores boolean flags as integers: 0 for false and 1 for true. If your model's toMap stores a Dart bool directly, the map may not match the database column expectations and queries or conversions can behave unexpectedly. Always convert booleans to integers when writing and convert integers back to booleans when reading. Another frequent mistake is forgetting to await database Futures; this can lead to UI code that reads stale data or tries to use a null Database before it is opened. Also watch primary keys: without a defined primary key you cannot reliably update or delete individual rows. Finally, avoid executing long-running database operations on the UI thread without awaiting them; make all database calls asynchronous and update the UI only after they complete. The better practice is to wrap database calls in try-catch to handle errors gracefully and to test migration paths before releasing an update. These small conversions and async discipline prevent many runtime surprises.

keyIdea.title: Pitfalls to avoid
keyIdea.text: Convert booleans to integers, await all database Futures, define a primary key, and test migrations carefully.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Booleans & Pitfalls
Boolean conversion
Convert booleans to integers for storage and back when reading.
// toMap
'isCompleted': isCompleted ? 1 : 0,

// fromMap
isCompleted: map['isCompleted'] == 1,
This conversion prevents mismatches and ensures consistent queries and model reconstruction.
Other common mistakes
  • Not awaiting database open or CRUD Futures, causing race conditions.
  • Forgetting a primary key, which prevents precise updates or deletes.
  • Mixing UI logic into the DatabaseHelper; keep separation of concerns.
  • Not testing onUpgrade migrations before shipping updates to users.
Pro tip
Wrap db calls in try-catch and log failures so you can recover or surface errors rather than silently losing data.

screens.title: Database migrations with onUpgrade
screens.subtitle: Evolving schema safely when releasing new app versions

narration.text: As your app grows you will change the schema: add columns, create new tables, or change constraints. To preserve user data across versions you implement migrations using the onUpgrade callback in openDatabase. The callback receives the database instance, the old version number, and the new version number. Use conditional checks like if (oldVersion < 2) to apply migration steps incrementally. A simple migration example is adding a new column: execute an ALTER TABLE statement to add the column with a sensible default or allow null if needed. Always test migrations against real sample data because ALTER TABLE operations are not always reversible and may behave differently across devices. Another pattern is to create a new table, copy transformed data into it, drop the old table, and rename the new table if more complex schema changes are required. Remember to increase the version number when releasing a schema change so onUpgrade will run for existing users. Finally, provide a rollback or a backup strategy during development to recover test data if a migration fails while you're iterating. Treat migrations as code: keep them in version-controlled routines and test them as part of your release checklist.

keyIdea.title: Migration rule
keyIdea.text: Use onUpgrade with version checks to apply ALTER TABLE or table-copy migrations and always test on real data.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Migrations
onUpgrade pattern
Run conditional SQL to evolve your schema when the version increases.
onUpgrade: (db, oldVersion, newVersion) async {
  if (oldVersion < 2) {
    await db.execute("ALTER TABLE todos ADD COLUMN dueDate TEXT");
  }
  if (oldVersion < 3) {
    await db.execute("CREATE TABLE tags(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, name TEXT)");
  }
}
Steps to follow:
  1. Increment database version when you release schema changes.
  2. Write conditional migration code for each version step.
  3. Test migrations against real sample databases before shipping.

screens.title: Integrating sqflite into the UI
screens.subtitle: Refactor your To-Do app to load, display, and update database-backed Todos

narration.text: Integrating sqflite into your Flutter UI means replacing the previous in-memory or shared_preferences flow with DatabaseHelper calls and ensuring the UI reflects the database state. In the Stateful widget, create a DatabaseHelper instance and an in-memory List. In initState call a _loadTodos method that awaits _dbHelper. getTodos and sets state. For add operations create a new Todo, await _dbHelper. insertTodo, then reload or append the returned item to the list to reflect the assigned id. For completion toggles create a new Todo with the updated isCompleted value, await updateTodo, and reload the list. For deletes await deleteTodo with the id, then remove the item from the in-memory list and call setState. A practical UI change is to replace the shared_preferences-backed ListView with ListTiles that show a Checkbox bound to Todo. isCompleted and an IconButton to delete. Remember to await the database operation before modifying UI state to avoid inconsistent displays. This integration step is the hands-on exercise: ensure the UI triggers the correct DatabaseHelper methods and that the ListView always reflects the persisted state. Integrating sqflite into the UI means ui widgets call databasehelper methods and update state only after awaiting results so the listview matches persisted data.. In practical terms, refactor your to-do app to load, display, and update database-backed todos. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: UI contract
keyIdea.text: UI widgets call DatabaseHelper methods and update state only after awaiting results so the ListView matches persisted data.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › UI Integration
State and loading
Use a DatabaseHelper instance and fetch todos in initState.
final DatabaseHelper _dbHelper = DatabaseHelper();
List<Todo> _todos = [];

@override
void initState() {
  super.initState();
  _loadTodos();
}

Future<void> _loadTodos() async {
  final todos = await _dbHelper.getTodos();
  setState(() => _todos = todos);
}
UI actions
Add, toggle, and delete operations that call DatabaseHelper methods and then reload or update state.
Future<void> _addTodo() async {
  final newTodo = Todo(title: _textController.text, description: 'No description yet');
  await _dbHelper.insertTodo(newTodo);
  _textController.clear();
  _loadTodos();
}

Future<void> _toggleTodoCompletion(Todo todo) async {
  final updated = Todo(id: todo.id, title: todo.title, description: todo.description, isCompleted: !todo.isCompleted);
  await _dbHelper.updateTodo(updated);
  _loadTodos();
}

Future<void> _removeTodo(int id) async {
  await _dbHelper.deleteTodo(id);
  _loadTodos();
}

screens.title: Hands-on: Refactor the To-Do app to use sqflite
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step instructions and a small checklist to verify your refactor

narration.text: This hands-on activity guides you to refactor your existing To-Do app to use sqflite. First, add sqflite and path_provider to pubspec. yaml and run flutter pub get. Next, create the Todo model with toMap and fromMap methods shown earlier, converting boolean fields to integers. Then implement DatabaseHelper as a singleton with an _initDatabase method that opens the file and creates the todos table. Replace any shared_preferences-based persistence with DatabaseHelper calls: in your stateful widget, instantiate DatabaseHelper, call getTodos in initState to load the initial list, and use insertTodo, updateTodo, and deleteTodo in response to UI actions. Add a Checkbox to each ListTile that toggles isCompleted by constructing an updated Todo and calling updateTodo. After each write operation, reload the list or update the local collection and setState. Verify the app by adding, toggling, and deleting todos and restarting the app to confirm persistence. The checklist at the end helps you ensure correctness: todos persist across restarts, checkboxes toggle and persist, deletes remove database rows, and no database operation is called before openDatabase completes. This exercise reinforces the model/helper separation and the async discipline required for robust local persistence.

keyIdea.text: Add dependencies, implement Todo model and DatabaseHelper, replace persistence calls, and verify persistence across restarts.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Three essential ideas from this chapter

narration.text: Let's review the three core concepts to carry forward. First, SQLite is a lightweight embedded relational database stored as a file on the device; choose it when you need structured records, queries, and stable identifiers. Second, the sqflite plugin is the Flutter interface for SQLite; combine it with path_provider to find a safe file location and use openDatabase with onCreate and onUpgrade callbacks to initialize and evolve your schema. Third, model classes with toMap and fromMap are central: convert booleans to integers, define a primary key, and keep serialization separate from S Q L logic. These building blocks — decision to use SQLite, a DatabaseHelper architecture, and disciplined model serialization — let you persist complex data reliably in a Flutter app. Keep practicing the hands-on refactor to reinforce the patterns and watch for the common pitfalls discussed earlier. Which one of these ideas will you apply first in your app?

keyIdea.title: Chapter summary
keyIdea.text: SQLite + sqflite provides structured local storage; use model mapping and a DatabaseHelper to keep persistence reliable.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Key Concepts
SQLite
A lightweight file-based relational database ideal for mobile apps that need structured, queryable storage.
sqflite
The Flutter plugin that provides async APIs to open and operate on SQLite databases from Dart code.
Model & CRUD
Use model classes with toMap/fromMap and implement insert, query, update, delete in a DatabaseHelper for clear separation of concerns.
Summary Takeaway

Structured local storage via sqflite is robust and lightweight; organize code into models and a DatabaseHelper, convert booleans to integers, and plan migrations to protect user data.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three quick reminders before you code

narration.text: A final quick set of reminders: always await database operations so your UI and storage stay in sync; convert Dart booleans to integers for SQLite storage and back when reading; and keep schema changes under version control with tested onUpgrade migrations. These habits protect your users' data and prevent common runtime issues. When you apply the hands-on challenge, focus first on correct mapping between model and table and then on making database operations asynchronous and awaited in your UI handlers. That sequence — correct model mapping, solid helper architecture, and disciplined async usage — is the practical recipe for reliable local data storage in Flutter.
